title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Chicago, IL: 6-Day Course
description: Prepare for the AWS CWI exam in Chicago with a six-day course: online or at your plant, built around structural steel, rail shops and refinery work.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Chicago: Six Days for Steel, Rail and Refinery Inspectors
html:
Chicago builds tall, sits where most of North America's large freight railroads meet, and refines crude oil at the southwest and southeast edges of the metro. Each of those industries depends on welds that somebody has to inspect against a code, and many of the people doing that inspecting started out as welders, fitters or quality technicians in Cook, Will, DuPage or Lake County. Atlantis NDT offers a six-day course that prepares those people for the AWS Certified Welding Inspector examination. A candidate studying alone takes the course online, at whatever pace a shift pattern allows, with a study plan, materials, practice questions and an instructor who answers questions by message. A plant, shop or contractor preparing several people at once can book the programme on its own premises as six consecutive working days. To price either version, send a Chicago quote request.

The credential itself comes only from AWS. AWS administers all three parts of the examination and awards the CWI to candidates who pass and satisfy its eligibility rules. What Atlantis sells is preparation. It holds no AWS approval or endorsement, plays no part in grading, and cannot see what will be on any candidate's exam. The questions used for practice were drafted by Atlantis from the subject areas AWS lists, so a good practice score is a sign of readiness, never a preview.

Chicago's welded economy: steel, rail and refining

Three industries account for most of the welding inspection demand around Chicago, and each favours a slightly different kind of inspector. Building and bridge work wants someone fluent in structural steel codes and comfortable on an erection floor in January. Rail work wants someone who understands repair welding on cars, trucks and locomotive frames and the records that go with it. Refinery work wants someone who can follow a piping specification, check a welder's qualification against the procedure on the job, and keep up with the pace of a turnaround. Around those three sit heavy-equipment manufacturers, steel service centres, tank and vessel shops, transit agencies and utilities. The sections below take each in turn, then cover the exam, the course, eligibility and what to do after you pass.

Building and bridge steel in a winter city

Chicago writes its own building code, and the current version is modelled on the International Building Code, which means structural steel welding on most commercial projects comes with special inspection requirements set by the engineer of record and accepted by the Department of Buildings. The code governing the welding is usually AWS D1.1. High-rise residential and office towers, hospital additions, data halls in the suburbs and large logistics buildings near the interstates all carry structural welding that has to be inspected in the shop and again after erection.

Bridges add a second code. Highway and transit bridge steel in Illinois comes out of shops working to AWS D1.5, which places tighter controls on procedures, consumables and fracture-critical members than D1.1 does. Fabricators that supply state and city bridge contracts need inspectors who know the difference and can explain it to a welder on the shop floor.

Weather is the local complication. D1.1 forbids welding when the ambient temperature is below 0°F, and it also bars welding on wet surfaces or in rain, snow or high wind unless the welder and the joint are protected. Preheat requirements rise with steel thickness and strength, so a heavy column splice in February needs heating before anyone strikes an arc. A Chicago inspector spends a surprising share of the winter checking temperature-indicating crayons and contact thermometers at the distance from the joint the code requires, confirming that tarps and heaters are actually working, and writing down what was measured. That habit of measuring and recording is exactly what the practical part of the CWI exam tests.

Rail: car shops, locomotives and the D15.1 option

Most of the big North American freight railroads meet in Chicago, and the region is full of the facilities that keep their fleets running: car repair shops, wheel and truck shops, locomotive maintenance facilities, and fabricators that build or rebuild hopper, tank and intermodal cars. Commuter and transit rail fleets add more maintenance welding on car bodies, underframes and bogies. Repair welding on rolling stock follows AWS D15.1, which covers welding on railroad cars and locomotives, together with each railroad's own engineering instructions.

That is unusual enough to matter for the exam. AWS currently offers D15.1 (2019 edition) as a Part C code book, so a candidate who already works in a car shop can sit the code portion in the book used every day instead of learning D1.1 from scratch. The course's code day can be built around D15.1 for those candidates, covering how the specification is laid out, where its tables live, and how its qualification and inspection requirements differ from structural work. Candidates who expect to move between rail and construction work often choose D1.1 instead, because it travels further. For context on how magnetic particle examination is used on rail components, see MT for the rail industry.

Refineries along the canal and the lakefront

The Chicago region has large refineries near Joliet and Lemont on the Illinois side and at Whiting, just across the Indiana line. Their maintenance programs and periodic turnarounds bring in large crews of contract welders for piping, exchanger and vessel work. Most of that piping follows ASME B31.3, and the welding procedures behind it are the owner's or contractor's, qualified under ASME Section IX; Atlantis does not write or qualify them. The welding inspector's job on a turnaround is to confirm that each welder is qualified for the procedure being used, that the procedure's essential variables are respected on the job, that fit-up, preheat and interpass limits are met, and that finished welds pass visual examination before they go to NDT.

B31.3 is one of the Part C options AWS offers, and refinery candidates often choose it. It is a dense document, and the Part C clock leaves little room for reading it cold, so the course spends the code day on its structure: where definitions, examination requirements and acceptance criteria sit, and how to move between the main text and the tables quickly. For more on the inspection methods used on refinery welds, see UT in refining and the guide to weld inspection NDT methods.

Who puts a CWI on the payroll in Chicagoland

  • Structural fabricators and erectors in the south and west suburbs and northwest Indiana, especially those supplying bridge work or certified to a fabricator quality program, which expect welding inspection on their own quality staff.
  • Testing laboratories and inspection firms that provide special inspection on building projects and quality assurance inspection on public works.
  • Railroads, car builders and car repair shops, where a CWI with D15.1 experience is a practical asset.
  • Refinery owners and turnaround contractors, who need inspectors for piping and pressure equipment repairs and hire heavily before planned outages.
  • Heavy-equipment and industrial manufacturers that weld frames, booms and pressure parts and want production weld quality checked against drawings and procedures.
  • Utilities and transit agencies, and the consulting engineers who represent them on construction contracts.

Sitting the AWS exam from Chicago

The examination is split three ways. Part A, the fundamentals paper, is 150 questions covering processes, metallurgy, testing, symbols, procedure documents, safety and calculations. Part B, the practical, pairs 46 questions with hands-on work: measuring and evaluating samples with inspection tools and working from procedure and qualification records. Part C is open-book: between 50 and 65 questions drawn from whichever code book the candidate picked. AWS sets a 72 percent minimum on every part.

Parts A and C are taken on a computer at a Prometric test centre; book the session once AWS has accepted your application and sent the eligibility code. Part B is different: AWS runs it at its own seminar and examination locations, and Chicago appears among the US cities where AWS currently holds its CWI seminars. Milwaukee and Indianapolis are on that list as well, which gives candidates in northern Illinois and northwest Indiana more than one option within driving distance. Confirm locations and dates on aws.org, since AWS adjusts them during the year.

Six days arranged around a Chicago work schedule

The national AWS CWI exam prep course page lays out the plan day by day. The first two days rebuild fundamentals: processes, joint design, symbols as AWS A2.4 presents them, the terminology of AWS A3.0, then metallurgy, mechanical testing, discontinuities and their causes, safety and the inspector's duties and ethics. The third day is practical measurement and visual acceptance, the skills behind Part B. The fourth works through the candidate's chosen code book for Part C. The fifth is timed practice exams for all three parts with a full review. The sixth goes back to weak areas, covers exam-day strategy, and checks the AWS application and supporting documents.

For a solo candidate in Chicago, the online format means the six days can be spread around rotating shifts, a turnaround, or a winter layoff. Nothing starts on a calendar date and nothing is broadcast; the candidate logs in, works the material, and sends questions to the instructor when stuck. For an employer, the on-site format puts the six days on the company's own premises with its own people. A rail shop or fabricator gains the most on the practical day, when candidates can use the company's fillet gauges, calipers and actual production weld samples rather than generic pictures. Atlantis has no training centre in Illinois and does not ship replica kits; on-site means your building and your tools.

Between study blocks, the free NDT practice tests help with the testing questions in Part A, and the Practical NDT welding workshop lets candidates rehearse inspection steps on screen. For realistic expectations about which part trips people up, read the breakdown of results by exam part.

Meeting the AWS eligibility rules

Eligibility is set by AWS QC1, the specification for certifying welding inspectors; AWS currently lists the 2016 edition with Amendment 1. The specification balances schooling against experience in welding-based work. A candidate with a high school diploma or an approved equivalent needs five years of that experience. An associate degree in welding, engineering, an engineering technology or a physical science brings the requirement down to two years, and a bachelor's degree in welding engineering or welding engineering technology brings it to one. Completed trade or vocational courses reduce it to four years, and engineering or technical coursework that counts toward a welding degree reduces it to three. Candidates whose schooling stopped at eighth grade need nine years, and those with less need twelve.

The application asks for proof. An employment verification form documents the experience, a Visual Acuity Exam Form documents the vision examination AWS requires, and the candidate supplies acceptable photo identification. Chicago candidates who came up through rail shops or union fabrication work sometimes undersell their experience on the form; describe the welding, fitting, supervision or inspection duties concretely, and let AWS decide what counts. The last course day reviews the paperwork, but the application, the vision examination and the exam fees remain the candidate's own business with AWS. The article on CWI requirements and career impact covers the rules in more depth.

Chicago welding schools and the AWS Chicago Section

AWS organises members into local sections grouped in districts. The Chicago Section sits in AWS District 13, alongside the Blackhawk, Illinois Valley, J.A.K. and Peoria sections. The Chicago Section's website lists its officers and scholarships, and it hosted the registration page for the 2026 AWS Midwest Districts Welding Conference. For a CWI candidate, section meetings are the easiest way to meet working inspectors, hear which employers are hiring, and find someone willing to read over an experience statement before it goes to AWS. Ask the section whether its technical programs earn professional development hours, since those count toward recertification later.

The welding trade itself is taught across the region's community colleges and vocational programs. Joliet Junior College, for example, runs a welding technology program in the heart of the refinery and logistics corridor southwest of the city. A welder who trains at a college like that, works several years in structural, rail or refinery welding, and keeps good records of it will reach AWS eligibility with an experience history that reads well on the application.

Where the CWI leads in Illinois

AWS keeps the CWI on a nine-year cycle. Renewals fall at year three and year six, and each renewal requires that you have not been out of practice or employment for more than two years within the previous three. At year nine you recertify, for instance by passing Part B again or by documenting 80 professional development hours, or through one of the other routes AWS lists. Inspectors who build enough experience can pursue Senior CWI, explained in the SCWI pathway article.

Many Chicago CWIs add NDT methods because bridge, building and refinery specifications call for magnetic particle or ultrasonic examination of welds that the CWI has already passed visually. Atlantis teaches NDT to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, under which certification is granted by your employer through its written practice rather than by any course. Useful starting points are VT Level 2 training, MT Level 2 training and the NDT training options for Chicago. Atlantis prepares candidates for API 510, 570 and 653 in separate self-paced online exam-prep courses. The comparison of the CWI, API 577 and ASNT Level II sets the three credentials side by side. Companies that need field inspection rather than training can look at weld inspection services in Chicago, magnetic particle testing in Chicago and ultrasonic testing in Chicago.

Getting a quote for Chicago

Tell us whether you are one candidate or a group, what each person does now, roughly how many years of welding-based experience they have, which Part C book they plan to use (D1.1, D1.5, D15.1 and B31.3 are the common Chicago choices), and when they hope to sit the exam. Employers booking on-site delivery should add the plant or shop address and whether a room, gauges and production samples are available. AWS sets its own exam, seminar and application charges and shows them on aws.org; to total those with travel and code books, try the CWI cost planner. Send the Chicago request; a reply comes within one business day.

For other Midwest options, see the Milwaukee CWI page and the Indianapolis CWI page, both cities where AWS also holds the practical.

faq.q: Is the CWI practical exam given in Chicago?
faq.a: AWS currently includes Chicago in its list of US CWI seminar cities, which is where Part B is administered. Milwaukee and Indianapolis are on the list too. Parts A and C are computer-based at Prometric centres. Check aws.org for current dates.

faq.q: Can I take Part C in the railroad code if I work in a car shop?
faq.a: Yes, AWS currently offers AWS D15.1 (2019 edition), the railroad welding specification for cars and locomotives, as a Part C code book. The course's code day can be built around it.

faq.q: Which Part C book do Chicago bridge fabricators usually want?
faq.a: Bridge shops work to AWS D1.5, which AWS offers for Part C. Building steel inspectors usually take D1.1, and refinery inspectors often choose ASME B31.3.

faq.q: Does cold weather change what a Chicago welding inspector checks?
faq.a: Yes. D1.1 bars welding below 0°F ambient and on wet or unprotected work, and preheat rises with thickness and strength. Inspectors verify preheat at the required distance from the joint and record it, a habit the Part B practical rewards.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Chicago?
faq.a: No. Candidates on their own study online with instructor support for questions. Employers can host the six-day programme at their own plant, shop or office.

faq.q: Is the course six days for online students as well?
faq.a: The content is the same six days. Online candidates spread it over whatever period suits their work, while on-site groups normally run it as six working days.

faq.q: How many years of experience do I need with a high school diploma?
faq.a: AWS QC1 currently asks for five years of welding-based work experience with a high school diploma or approved equivalent. Formal welding or engineering education reduces that.

faq.q: Can a Chicago rail shop or fabricator host the course for its own welders?
faq.a: Yes. Send the number of candidates, their roles, the code book they need and your address through the quote form. On the practical day your candidates can work with the shop's own gauges and production welds. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: What NDT training pairs well with a CWI in Illinois?
faq.a: Visual testing first, then magnetic particle and ultrasonic methods, trained to ASNT SNT-TC-1A with certification granted by your employer. See NDT training for Chicago.
